name: Cloud Computing Basics
objectives: Given a list of everyday apps and a small business example, explain what cloud computing is and name its main benefits and risks, in your own words, with at least two benefits and one risk
Given six cloud services, sort each one into SaaS, PaaS or IaaS and say what you are responsible for in each, getting at least 5 of 6 right
Using Google Drive or OneDrive, create a folder, add two files and give them clear names, without help, so another person could find each file by its name
Given a file and a person to share it with, share the file with the least access needed, check who has access and remove access, with no file left open to people who do not need it
In your own Google or Microsoft account, turn on two-step verification, review signed-in devices and spot a phishing message, before the final task is finished

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The cloud in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Explain in your own words what cloud computing is.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of everyday apps and a small business example, you will explain what cloud computing is and name its main benefits and risks, in your own words, with at least two benefits and one risk.
"The cloud" means computers in large buildings called data centers that you use over the internet. Instead of keeping everything on your own phone or laptop, your files, apps and computing power live on those computers, and you reach them from any device.
Think of electricity. You do not build a power plant at home; you plug in and pay for what you use. Cloud computing works the same way: a company owns the computers, and people and businesses use what they need, when they need it.
Everyday examples: Gmail and Outlook email, Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud and Dropbox for files, Netflix and Spotify for streaming, and AI assistants like ChatGPT or Copilot, which run on cloud computers.
Words to know:
- Cloud computing: using computers, storage and software over the internet instead of on your own device.
- Data center: a large building full of computers that run cloud services.
- Server: a powerful computer that provides a service to other computers over a network.
Try it now: List five apps or websites you used this week. Next to each, write "cloud" if your stuff is stored or run on the company's computers rather than only on your device.
You can now explain cloud computing in your own words and point to cloud services you already use.

check.q: Where do your files live when you save them to the cloud?
options: On computers in a data center that you reach over the internet
Only inside your phone's memory card
On a disc you mail to the company
In your phone's text messages
check.why: The cloud is computers in data centers that you use over the internet from any device.

check.q: A friend asks why the cloud is like electricity. What do you say?
options: Both stop working at night
Both need a cable to your house
You use what you need without owning the computers, like power without a power plant
Both are free for everyone
check.why: The lesson compares the cloud to plugging in and paying for power without building a power plant.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Why people and businesses use the cloud
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main benefits and risks of the cloud.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of everyday apps and a small business example, you will explain what cloud computing is and name its main benefits and risks, in your own words, with at least two benefits and one risk.
Benefits: you can get to your files from any device; a lost phone does not mean lost photos; teams can work on the same document at once; and businesses can start small and grow, paying for more computing only when they need it, instead of buying expensive servers.
Risks: you need an internet connection; if someone steals your password, they can reach your files from anywhere; free plans have storage limits; and your data is held by a company, so you should know its privacy settings.
Big cloud providers for businesses include Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. For everyday people, Google, Microsoft, Apple and Dropbox offer free cloud storage with paid upgrades. Check each company's own page for the current free storage amount.
Words to know:
- Scalability: the ability to grow or shrink computing power as needed.
- Provider: the company that runs the cloud service.
- Storage limit: the most data your plan lets you keep.
Try it now: Think of a small business you know, like a barbershop, food truck or church office. Write two ways the cloud could help it and one risk it should plan for.
You can now name the main benefits and risks of the cloud and the big cloud providers.

check.q: Which is a benefit of keeping your photos in the cloud?
options: You never need the internet
A lost phone does not mean lost photos
Free plans have no storage limits
No company ever holds your data
check.why: Cloud copies stay safe on the provider's computers even if the phone is lost.

check.q: A food truck owner wants to move records to the cloud. What risk should they plan for first?
options: The cloud makes files bigger
The cloud only works on one device
Cloud files cannot be shared with staff
Someone with a stolen password could reach the files from anywhere
check.why: A stolen password opens cloud files from anywhere, so strong account security matters.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: SaaS, PaaS and IaaS: the three service types
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Sort cloud services into SaaS, PaaS and IaaS.
This lesson builds toward: Given six cloud services, you will sort each one into SaaS, PaaS or IaaS and say what you are responsible for in each, getting at least 5 of 6 right.
Cloud services come in three main types, depending on how much the provider does for you. Use a pizza example: you can buy a ready pizza, rent a kitchen with ingredients, or rent just the oven.
SaaS (Software as a Service): finished software you use in a browser or app, like Gmail, Google Docs, Microsoft 365 or Zoom. The provider runs everything. PaaS (Platform as a Service): a ready platform where developers build and run their own apps without managing servers, like Google App Engine or Azure App Service. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): raw virtual computers, storage and networks you set up yourself, like Amazon EC2 or Azure Virtual Machines.
In every type, security is shared. The provider protects its data centers; you are always responsible for your own password, who you share with, and what you upload.
Step by step:
- Ask: do I just use finished software? That is SaaS.
- Do I build my own app on a ready platform? That is PaaS.
- Do I set up my own virtual computers? That is IaaS.
- In all three, protect your own account and data.
Words to know:
- SaaS: Software as a Service: finished software you use over the internet.
- PaaS: Platform as a Service: a ready platform for building and running your own apps.
- IaaS: Infrastructure as a Service: virtual computers, storage and networks you rent and manage.
- Shared responsibility: the provider secures the cloud; you secure your account and data in it.
Try it now: Sort these into SaaS, PaaS or IaaS: Gmail, Azure Virtual Machines, Google App Engine, Zoom, Amazon EC2, Microsoft 365. Check your answers against the examples in this lesson.
You can now sort cloud services into SaaS, PaaS and IaaS and explain shared responsibility.

check.q: Google App Engine lets developers run their own apps without managing servers. Which type is it?
options: SaaS
IaaS
PaaS
None of the three types
check.why: A ready platform where developers build and run apps is Platform as a Service.

check.q: Your school uses Microsoft 365, which is SaaS. What is still your job?
options: Protecting your own password and choosing who you share with
Guarding the data center building
Fixing the provider's servers
Nothing; SaaS means the provider does everything
check.why: Security is shared: the provider runs the service, but your password and sharing are always yours.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Storing and organizing files in cloud storage
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Upload, create and organize files in Google Drive or OneDrive.
This lesson builds toward: Using Google Drive or OneDrive, you will create a folder, add two files and give them clear names, without help, so another person could find each file by its name.
Google Drive comes with a free Google account, and OneDrive comes with a free Microsoft account. Both work in a web browser (drive.google.com or onedrive.com) and as phone apps from the official app store.
Use the New button to create a folder or a document, or Upload to add a file from your device. Give files clear names, like "Resume - Jordan Lee - 2026", so you can find them later. Put related files into folders.
Syncing keeps a file the same on every device: change it on your laptop and the new version appears on your phone. Many cloud services also keep older versions, so you can go back if you make a mistake.
Step by step:
- Sign in at drive.google.com or onedrive.com (or open the app).
- Press New and choose Folder; name it clearly.
- Open the folder; press New to create a document, or Upload to add a file.
- Rename files with clear names.
- Open the same file on another device to see it sync.
Words to know:
- Upload: copy a file from your device to the cloud.
- Sync: keep files the same on all your devices automatically.
- Version history: older saved copies of a file you can go back to.
Try it now: In Google Drive or OneDrive, create a folder called "Career Documents". Create or upload two files into it and give them clear names. Then open the folder on a second device if you have one.
You can now upload, create, name and organize files in cloud storage and know they sync across devices.

check.q: What does "sync" do for a file in OneDrive?
options: Deletes the old copy every night
Keeps the same version of the file on all your devices
Sends the file to everyone in your contacts
Turns the file into a PDF
check.why: Syncing keeps a file the same on every device you use.

check.q: You saved a cover letter as "doc1". What should you do so you can find it later?
options: Leave it; search will guess
Make a new folder for every file
Upload it again with the same name
Rename it clearly, like "Cover Letter - Jordan Lee - 2026"
check.why: Clear names make files easy to find later.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Sharing files safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Share a file with the right person and the right level of access, and remove access.
This lesson builds toward: Given a file and a person to share it with, you will share the file with the least access needed, check who has access and remove access, with no file left open to people who do not need it.
Cloud files are easy to share, which is useful and risky. Press Share on a file and add a person's email address, or copy a link. Choose what they can do: view, comment or edit.
Give the least access needed. A résumé for an employer: view only. A group project: edit for your team. Be careful with links set so that "anyone with the link" can open the file; anyone who gets the link can see it, even if it is forwarded.
Check who has access from the Share or Manage access screen, and remove people when a project ends. Never put files with Social Security numbers, bank details or passwords in a shared folder.
Step by step:
- Select the file and press Share.
- Add the person's email, or copy a link.
- Choose View, Comment or Edit; pick the least they need.
- Avoid "anyone with the link" for private files.
- Later, open Share or Manage access and remove people who no longer need it.
Words to know:
- Permission level: what someone can do with your file: view, comment or edit.
- Least access: giving people only the access they truly need.
Try it now: Share one file from your "Career Documents" folder with a friend or family member as view-only. Ask them to open it. Then open Manage access and remove them.
You can now share a cloud file with the right permission level and remove access when it is no longer needed.

check.q: Which sharing setting gives the least access?
options: Edit
Comment
View
Owner
check.why: View lets people open the file but not change it, which is the least access.

check.q: Your group project is finished and four classmates still have edit access. What do you do?
options: Open Manage access and remove the people who no longer need it
Change the link to "anyone with the link"
Delete your whole account
Leave it in case they need it someday
check.why: Remove access when a project ends so only people who need the file can reach it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping your cloud account secure
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn on two-step verification and review your account's security.
This lesson builds toward: In your own Google or Microsoft account, you will turn on two-step verification, review signed-in devices and spot a phishing message, before the final task is finished.
Your cloud account holds your files, email and photos, so it is a target. The most important step is two-step verification (also called two-factor or multi-factor authentication): after your password, you also confirm with your phone. A thief with only your password cannot get in.
Use a long, unique password, ideally kept in a password manager. Google and Microsoft both have a security check-up page in your account settings that shows devices signed in, recent activity and recovery options.
Watch for phishing: fake emails saying "your storage is full" or "someone shared a file with you" that lead to a fake sign-in page. Go to drive.google.com or onedrive.com yourself rather than clicking. Remember shared responsibility: the provider protects its data centers; you protect your account.
Step by step:
- Open your Google or Microsoft account security settings.
- Turn on two-step verification.
- Check recovery phone and email are correct.
- Review signed-in devices and remove any you do not know.
- Go to cloud sites yourself instead of clicking email links.
Words to know:
- Two-step verification: a second check, like a code or a tap on your phone, after your password.
- Password manager: an app that creates and stores strong passwords for you.
- Phishing: a fake message that tries to trick you into giving your password.
Try it now: Final task practice: open your Google or Microsoft account's security settings, turn on two-step verification, and review signed-in devices. Then finish the final task with your "Career Documents" folder.
You can now protect your cloud account with two-step verification, a security check-up and phishing awareness.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Folder and files No "Career Documents" folder, or the files have unclear names like "doc1". The folder holds two files with clear names. The files are also opened on a second device to show they sync. Safe sharing The file was shared with edit access or as "anyone with the link", or access was never removed. One file was shared view-only, access was checked, then removed. Can explain why view-only was the least access needed. Account protected Two-step verification is off. Two-step verification is on and signed-in devices were reviewed. Recovery phone and email were also checked, and the learner can name one phishing warning sign. The cloud explained The three sentences are missing or do not say what the cloud is. Three clear sentences say what the cloud is and give a benefit and a risk. The sentences also use an everyday comparison, like electricity. Service types One or more of the SaaS, PaaS and IaaS examples is wrong or missing. One correct example each of SaaS, PaaS and IaaS. Also says what the user is still responsible for under shared responsibility. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

options: Typing your password twice
Having two different email accounts
Saving your password in two places
A second check, often on your phone, after your password
check.why: After the password, you also confirm with your phone, so a thief with only the password cannot get in.

check.q: You see a phone you do not recognize in your account's signed-in devices. What do you do?
options: Ignore it; it is probably fine
Remove it and change your password
Share your password with it
Turn off two-step verification
check.why: Removing unknown devices in a security check-up keeps strangers out of your account.
